summary: Create tiered channel-provisioning policy and bot-access lifecycle for cross-pod integrations
description:
Issue summary:
We need a formalized provisioning policy and automation for creating cross-pod Slack channels and associated Confluence space links that enforces permission propagation, bot access tiers, and automated lifecycle (archival/retention). This is driven by recurring mistakes where channels are created without appropriate guest constraints or bot scopes, causing audits and noisy integrations.

Impact:
- Risk of overexposed channels with guests who should not have access to private Confluence docs.
- Support load from manual permission changes and emergency audits.
- Potential non-compliance with retention rules for sensitive pods.

Desired outcome:
- A templated channel provisioning flow that applies conditional permission sets based on pod classification (internal, partner, vendor).
- Bot access tiers (read-only, post-only, admin) that are granted automatically according to template and timebound leases.
- Automatic propagation of a channel metadata tag to any created Confluence page or linked doc and to Jira project permissions where applicable.
- Pre-provision validation webhook that blocks creation if the requested permission set violates pod policy.

Acceptance criteria (see acceptance_criteria field): policies and automation are documented, deployed in staging, and pass test plan.

Additional context and constraints:
- This ties to existing audit requirements for vendor partners; channels that include vendor guests must default to "restricted-guest" template.
- Automation must integrate with the existing bot service account used by platform-ops and respect SCIM groups from Okta.
- Where a channel is created with a long-lived bot-admin role, the system must create an expiration lease and create a Jira task for manual review 7 days before expiry.

References:
- Slack naming convention doc: confluence.redwood.internal/display/OPS/Slack+Naming+Standards
- Compliance retention matrix: confluence.redwood.internal/display/SEC/Retention+Matrix
acceptance_criteria: Provisioning template types defined: internal, partner, vendor, ephemeral
Bot-access tiers defined and enforced: read-only, post-only, admin with lease metadata
Pre-provision webhook rejects requests that would grant guest access to restricted pods
Channel metadata tag is propagated to new Confluence pages and included on created Jira projects
Automation creates a Jira review task 7 days before bot-admin lease expiry
Documentation and runbook published in Confluence and linked from the provisioning UI
proposed_rbac: Suggested mapping: pod-classification -> permission template. internal: @pod-members (full), bots -> post-only; partner: @pod-members (limited), guests -> restricted, bots -> post-only with lease; vendor: channel defaults to guest-restricted, bots -> read-only; ephemeral: auto-archive 30d, limited retention. Use Okta group attributes to populate @pod-members. Bot service account uses scoped OAuth tokens per-template.
rollout_plan: 1) Create templates and validation webhook in staging; 2) Run a 2-week pilot with Platform-Integrations pod; 3) Monitor audit logs and error rate; 4) Gradual enablement with an opt-in toggle per team for 2 weeks; 5) Full enforcement; 6) Post-rollout audit and retrospective. Rollback: disable webhook enforcement and revert to manual provisioning. Communicate changes to teams and provide self-service request form.
test_plan: Create channel with 'vendor' template and verify guest restrictions and Confluence tag propagation
Simulate bot-admin lease creation and confirm Jira review task and reminder triggers
Attempt to create channel violating pod policy and confirm webhook blocks request with clear error
Verify Okta group mapping correctly assigns @pod-members in 3 sample pods
Confirm archival runs at configured TTL for ephemeral template and archives Confluence links appropriately
